title: The Substitute Teacher
description: Your favorite teacher has been suddenly transferred. After hours, you slip into the empty staff room to find out why.
reflection_prompt: Which clue changed your theory about what really happened, and what did you almost overlook?

exits.label: Down the corridor to Ms. Banerjee's classroom

hotspots.label: A bookshelf with something behind it
A folded note on a desk

puzzles.prompt: You pick up the letter. It is addressed to the Principal. Look carefully at the signature block — who filed this complaint against Ms. Banerjee?
options: A parent of a student in Ms. Banerjee's class
The school board or District Education Officer
It is anonymous — no name or signature
puzzles.explanation_correct: The letter is signed by Aarav's parent — a private individual, not the school board. The complaint was filed after Ms. Banerjee intervened in a home matter to protect Aarav. This is a key piece of evidence: the transfer was triggered by a parental complaint, not an official administrative decision.
puzzles.explanation_wrong: Look again at the bottom of the letter. There is a printed name and address — that belongs to a parent, not to any official body. Anonymous complaints would not carry the weight needed to force a transfer.

puzzles.prompt: The staff phone has three saved voicemails. Listen to each one. Which message best explains why Ms. Banerjee was transferred so suddenly?
transcripts: Voicemail 1 — Principal Sharma, dry and formal: 'Ms. Banerjee, your transfer order is effective this Friday. Please hand over class records to the front office by Thursday evening. That will be all.'

Voicemail 2 — Unknown parent voice, irritated: 'I spoke to Principal Sharma again today. I have made it very clear that my family's donations to this school come with certain expectations. What happens in my home is not a teacher's business. I expect this to be handled.'

Voicemail 3 — Mrs. Iyer, a fellow teacher, voice hushed and worried: 'Deepa — it's Sunita. I know about the complaint. I know why they're moving you. I tried to speak to Sharma but she wouldn't hear it. I'm worried about Aarav. Please call me before you leave. Don't let this just disappear.'
options: Voicemail 2 — The parent's pressure on the school
Voicemail 3 — Mrs. Iyer's worried message about Aarav
puzzles.explanation_correct: Mrs. Iyer's message is the most revealing. She confirms the complaint exists, suggests the principal refused to listen, and most importantly, she names Aarav directly and expresses worry about him. The other messages confirm the transfer happened and who pushed for it — but only this message tells you *why it matters* and that someone else already suspects it is wrong.
puzzles.explanation_wrong: That message tells you part of the story, but it is not the one that explains the full picture. Voicemail 3 from Mrs. Iyer is the most complete account — she names Aarav, confirms the complaint, and signals that the transfer is being treated as a quiet way to make a problem disappear.

puzzles._engine_todo: ordering type not yet supported by engine — authored as factual with single-best-answer. True ordering data preserved in ordering_items for future engine upgrade.
puzzles.prompt: Five printed emails are scattered on the desk, out of order. Based on dates, references, and the tone of each message, which email came FIRST in this chain — the one that started everything?

ordering_items.text: Email from Ms. Banerjee to Principal Sharma (Mon): 'I am writing to flag a concern regarding one of my students, Aarav. I have observed signs that may indicate stress at home. I would like to request a brief meeting to discuss appropriate support. — D. Banerjee'

Email from Principal Sharma to Ms. Banerjee (Tue): 'Ms. Banerjee, I appreciate your concern, but I must caution you about overstepping. Parents are our stakeholders. Please focus on academics and allow pastoral matters to be handled through proper channels. — Principal Sharma'

Email from Aarav's parent to Principal Sharma (Wed): 'I have been informed by my son that his class teacher, Ms. Banerjee, has been asking him personal questions about our family. This is completely unacceptable and a violation of our privacy. I expect immediate action. — [Parent's name]'

Email from Principal Sharma to District Office (Thu): 'I wish to request a transfer for one of our teachers, Ms. Deepa Banerjee, effective end of this month. Reason: professional conduct concerns. I will provide documentation on request.'

Email from District Office to Principal Sharma (Fri): 'Transfer approved. Ms. Banerjee to report to Government Senior Secondary School, Sector 14, effective next Monday. Please arrange handover of responsibilities.'

options: Email A — Ms. Banerjee's concern about Aarav to the Principal
Email B — Principal Sharma's warning to Ms. Banerjee
Email C — The parent's complaint to the Principal
Email D — Principal Sharma's transfer request to the District Office
Email E — The District Office's approval of the transfer
puzzles.explanation_correct: Ms. Banerjee's email to the Principal was the first. She noticed something concerning about Aarav and tried to raise it through official channels — the right thing to do. Everything else followed from that single act of care: the Principal's warning, the parent's complaint, the transfer request, the approval. The sequence is important: the transfer was not random or administrative, it was a direct response to Ms. Banerjee doing her job.
puzzles.explanation_wrong: That email was not the first. The chain started with Ms. Banerjee herself raising a safeguarding concern about Aarav with the Principal. Putting the emails in order — A, B, C, D, E — shows how one teacher's act of care was systematically reversed by pressure from a parent with influence.

puzzles.prompt: You hold Aarav's drawing up to the light. It is a pencil sketch — a house, two adult figures, a smaller figure standing apart. The smaller figure's face has no expression. What does this drawing tell you?
options: It is just a house — a typical drawing exercise from an art class
There is conflict at home — the adults look tense, the child looks isolated
This is a happy memory — Aarav drew the school building and his family visiting for an event

puzzles.prompt: Ms. Banerjee's handwritten comments fill the margins of Aarav's homework notebook. One comment directly contradicts what the complaint letter claims about her 'interference'. Which margin note is it?
options: 'Good effort on the essay, Aarav. Your writing is improving — keep practising the opening paragraph.' (Written in red ink, dated three weeks ago.)

'Aarav — you mentioned something in class today that I did not want to forget. My door is always open if you need to talk. — Ms. B' (Written in blue ink, dated the day before her first email to the Principal.)
'Please redo questions 4 and 5. Show your working. I know you can do better than this.' (Written in red ink, no date.)
puzzles.explanation_correct: This note is dated the day before Ms. Banerjee wrote to the Principal. It shows she did not insert herself into Aarav's home life uninvited — she responded to something *Aarav himself said* in class. The complaint claimed she was prying; this note shows she was listening and following up with care. That is the contradiction.
puzzles.explanation_wrong: That note is about academics. Look for the note that is dated and personal — one that shows a connection between something Aarav said and Ms. Banerjee's decision to contact the Principal. The timing matters.

puzzles.prompt: A folded piece of paper sits on a desk near the back row. It looks like it was passed between students. Do you read it?
options: Read it — understanding what is happening matters more than privacy right now
Leave it folded — it is not your note to read, no matter what is inside

climax.modal_text: You hear footsteps in the corridor outside. The lights at the far end flick on. Principal Sharma is back early. You have seconds to decide. The evidence you have found is in your hands. Do you knock on her door?

options.label: Walk away quietly — leave everything as you found it
Tell another teacher in general terms — let the adults sort it out
Slip a note under Mrs. Iyer's door naming Aarav — no confrontation
options.gating_message: Collect at least 4 pieces of evidence to unlock this path.

options.label: Knock on Principal Sharma's door and present what you found
options.gating_message: Solve the evidence board with 7 or more pieces of evidence to unlock this path.

p1_complaint: The letter has two important parts — the body and the signature block at the bottom. Both are worth reading carefully.
Ignore the school letterhead at the top — that is just where it was received, not who wrote it. Focus on the name and address printed at the end of the letter.
The letter is signed by Aarav's parent. The correct answer is option A: a parent filed this complaint, not the school board, and it was not anonymous.
p2_voicemails: Each voicemail tells you something different. One is official, one is threatening, one is worried. Which voice is most concerned about Aarav himself?
The first message is administrative. The second message tells you who applied pressure. But only one message specifically names Aarav and expresses worry about what happens to him next.
Voicemail 3 from Mrs. Iyer is the key. She confirms the complaint, says the Principal refused to act, and asks Ms. Banerjee not to let the situation disappear. Select option C.
p3_email_thread: The emails have dates on them. Try reading the oldest date first — what set the whole chain in motion?
Ms. Banerjee wrote the very first email — she noticed something about Aarav and flagged it to the Principal. Everything that came after was a reaction to that one act of care.

The correct first email is option A: Ms. Banerjee's concern email to Principal Sharma, dated Monday. The full order is A (concern) → B (warning) → C (parent complaint) → D (transfer request) → E (approval).
p4_drawing: Look at where each figure is standing in relation to the others, and at Aarav's figure in particular. What does the body language and positioning suggest?

The adult figures are positioned close together, and the smaller figure stands apart. The child's face has no expression drawn in — that absence is deliberate. What emotion does that negative space communicate?
p5_notebook: You are looking for a note that shows Ms. Banerjee was responding to something Aarav said, not inserting herself uninvited. Check the dates on each note — timing matters here.

The complaint says Ms. Banerjee was 'prying'. A note written the day before her email to the Principal would show whether that is true — did she act on her own initiative, or did she respond to Aarav?

The correct note is option B — written in blue ink, dated the day before Ms. Banerjee's first email to the Principal. It shows she wrote 'my door is always open' in direct response to something Aarav mentioned in class, not because she was prying.
p6_folded_note: Think about who this note belongs to and what reading it without permission means — even if the information inside might help someone.

Both choices have real consequences. Reading it may reveal a clue but raises a question about privacy. Leaving it folded respects privacy but means you act on incomplete information. Neither choice is simply right or wrong.
evidence_board: Try sorting what you have into three groups: things the Principal would say happened, things you believe actually happened based on the full picture, and anything that does not quite fit either story.

The complaint letter and the transfer notice belong to the principal's version of events. The voicemails, emails, and Aarav's drawing and notebook note belong to what actually happened. The staff-room key is a practical item — it does not tell you anything about the complaint.

Correct groupings: complaint_letter and transfer_notice go into 'principal_says'. The voicemail transcripts (especially 2 and 3), the email sequence, child_drawing, and notebook_note go into 'actually_happened'. The staff_room_key goes into 'irrelevant' — it was useful for access but is not evidence about Ms. Banerjee's transfer.

compliant_bystander.title: You Walked Away
paragraphs: You slip out of the staff room before Principal Sharma reaches the corridor. The door clicks shut behind you. You walk home through the school gate, the evidence still turning over in your mind. No one saw you. No one knows what you found.

The next morning, a substitute teacher stands at the front of Ms. Banerjee's classroom. Her name is written in neat capitals on the board. At lunch, you see Aarav sitting alone at the end of a table, staring at his food. He does not eat.
Some things stay with you even when you do nothing. This is one of them. There is no shame in choosing safety — but the question of what you could have done will sit with you for a while.

cautious_investigator.title: You Passed It On
paragraphs: You find your class teacher the next morning and tell them, carefully, that you think something is not right about Ms. Banerjee's transfer. You do not mention breaking in. You do not name Aarav. You just say: 'I think someone needs to look into it.'

Your teacher nods slowly and says they will look into it. Maybe they will. You watch the next few weeks for signs — a meeting, a change, anything. The substitute teacher stays. Aarav seems quieter than usual but not worse.
Passing information up the chain is a reasonable thing to do when you are not sure what to do with it yourself. You flagged it. Whether adults act on it is now in their hands — and outside yours.

quiet_protector.title: You Helped from the Shadows
paragraphs: You find a sheet of paper and write Mrs. Iyer's name on the envelope — you remember it from the voicemail. You write two short lines: 'Aarav needs support. Ms. Banerjee was not wrong.' You fold it, slide it under the door of the staff room closest to Mrs. Iyer's name on the noticeboard, and walk away.

Two weeks later, you notice Aarav walking to school with Mrs. Iyer's class for a visit to the school garden. He is talking. His shoulders look less tight. Ms. Banerjee does not come back — but something changed.

You did not confront anyone. You did not put yourself at risk. But you made sure the right person had the right information. That kind of quiet care has its own strength — it is called empathy in action.

whistleblower.title: You Spoke the Truth
paragraphs: You knock on Principal Sharma's door. She opens it, startled to see a student. You place the evidence on her desk — the emails in sequence, the notebook note, the drawing. You say: 'I think Ms. Banerjee was transferred because she was trying to protect a student. I think that was wrong.' Your voice shakes, but you do not stop.

Principal Sharma asks how you got in. You tell her. She calls your parents. It is uncomfortable and frightening and takes several weeks to resolve. But the District Board reviews the case. Ms. Banerjee is reinstated three weeks later. Aarav's family is referred to the school counsellor.

At school, some students say you got a teacher in trouble. Others quietly say thank you. The pushback is real. But so is the outcome. Courage does not mean having no fear — it means going ahead despite the fear. You did that today.
